before: XI. Canons are to be observed concerning good angels and their governance. First, the confirmation of angels in the good was not a wages owed to some merit, but the free reward of most liberal God (Romans 11:35). Second, angels serve each person and each order (Psalm 34:8). Third, a human being has not only one guardian angel but many at once (Psalm 91:11; Matthew 18:10; Acts 12:15; Zanchi). Fourth, angels are not to be adored (Revelation 19:10). Fifth, angels turn away from whatever smells of vice; yet among vices they most hate heat, smoke, and stench — the heat of anger and envy, the smoke of pride, the stench of luxury.

before: V. The death of Christ is the true separation of His soul from the body. Hence the Jews are rightly said to have killed Him (Acts 3:14).
VI. The burial of Christ is a sure confirmation of that death.

VII. His descent to the lower regions is His state from the time of burial until the resurrection, in which He is judged to have been under the dominion of death. This state was especially necessary, both that He might render obedience to His Father, and that, tempted in all things yet without sin, He might be able to sympathize with those who are tempted, and finally that through sufferings He might be consecrated as priest and king, and so enter into the glory of His kingdom. See Sanford and Parker in their most learned books on the descent to hell.

before: But since being is divided into substance and accident: God is so being that He is substance as much as possible, because He most of all subsists through Himself and depends on nothing at all, but from Himself, in Himself, and through nothing other than through Himself is whatever He is. But every accident presupposes another being by which it is sustained: yet God, since He exists from Himself, is necessarily the first being, and therefore cannot be sustained by another prior being.

NEXT, God is here called the highest being, that is, leaving all the rest behind Himself in perfection, as being their cause. For every principal cause of which we treat here, if it produce an effect of a diverse ratio from itself (which here must necessarily happen), is nobler than that effect; which is demonstrated in the Metaphysics. And hence it is that Dionysius said things are like God, but not God like things, since He exceeds above, and they have from God that they imitate Him, not the reverse (Isaiah 40:17-18; Romans 1:23).

THIRD, since two things chiefly contain the essential perfection of substances, namely essence and life — that of all, this of some, beyond which the human mind can comprehend nothing in them — therefore, as essence, so also life is most deservedly attributed to God, by which namely He is active in Himself and outside Himself; and without which He cannot be the cause of the other things, as will be demonstrated below. For this reason God in the Scriptures is everywhere called being and living (Revelation 1:8 and 4:8; Deuteronomy; Psalm 18:47; 84:3; Jeremiah 10:10; Ezekiel 33:11; Daniel 4:34; Matthew 16:16; John 5:26 and 6:57; Acts 14:15; Romans 9:26). FOURTH, since life belongs to God as first and highest being in the most perfect manner, and therefore spiritual, we deservedly consider integrity in it, which is contained in virtue and beatitude (Psalm 25; 1 Timothy 6:15). LASTLY, the word independent is added in the description, which here stands in place of a difference, and discriminates God from created things, and signifies that both essence and life are so in God that He has each not from elsewhere but from Himself (Exodus 3:14; Psalm 36:10). From all which it is firmly gathered that nature is rightly attributed to God, that word taken in a looser significate, so that it notes the same as Deity itself (Colossians 2:9) — namely that through which God is God and differs from all other things. Hence Paul (Galatians 4:8): Not knowing God, he says, you served those who by nature are not gods — indicating that He alone is the true God who is God by nature, that is, who has a truly divine essence and persons.

before: I demonstrate that God is properly eternal — that is, without beginning or end, never about to cease. before: IN THE FIRST PLACE, Being is here put in the place of a genus, and is rightly said of God. For God is in the most perfect manner, because He exists from Himself, as we showed in chapter 2. And hence He imposed on Himself a name from that which is to be (Exodus 3:14), by which He declares that He is BEING SIMPLY, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. For so He discerns Himself from others that He says Himself to be simply, but signifies that the rest in a manner are not (Isaiah 40:15, 17; Psalm 62:10).

Yet Being is not said of God altogether in the same way as of creatures. For the ratio of being in God infinitely exceeds that which is in creatures: from which Being is predicated of God and creatures not univocally but analogically — since these are not called beings except by attribution to Him from whom they have it that they are and are called beings. God therefore most properly and substantially is being. Nor do we destroy unity when we say God is being. For the copula here does not couple diverse things, nor several according to the thing, but according to formal rationes conceived by us, and in divine propositions is always taken essentially.
God Himself revealed to Moses that this is His name: I am who I am. Afterwards He said, the LORD your God, God is one. Therefore it is to be established that nothing is said of God more essentially.

before: II. The attributes of God are proper or figurative. The proper attributes of God are of three genera. Some are as of being; others as of living virtually; others as of living integrally.

Those belong to God simply, with respect to essence, insofar as He is in the supreme mode; these evidently, with respect to intelligent life, insofar as He understands, wills, acts, and works; these excellently, with respect to virtue and beatitude, insofar as He acts well and blessedly. This is proved jointly and separately. Jointly, by the words TRUE and LIVING (Jeremiah 10:10; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; Revelation 1:17-18). Separately, with respect to essence (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 44:6; Revelation 1:8 and 21:6 and 22:13); with respect to spiritual life (Deuteronomy 32:40; Judges 8:19; 1 Samuel 25:34; Psalm 18:47; 84:3; John 4:24; 1 Timothy 1:17; Colossians 1:15); with respect to integrity (Deuteronomy 32:4; Matthew 5:48).

before: But that God lives we prove thus. FIRST, from the clear testimonies of sacred Scripture. For this distinctly attributes life to Him: Genesis 16:14; Numbers 14:21; Deuteronomy 32:40; 1 Samuel 17:26; Psalm 36:10; Psalm 42:3; Jeremiah 4:2; Ezekiel 33:11; Matthew 16:16; Acts 14:15; Romans 9:26; Hebrews 3:12; Hebrews 10:31.

SECOND, from God's infinite perfection. Whoever is of infinite perfection lives. God is of infinite perfection. Therefore God lives. THIRD, from God's inward actions. Whoever understands, wills, and can, lives. God understands, wills, can. Therefore God lives.

FOURTH, from God's inward actions commonly called ad intra. Whoever is begetting and begotten, breathing and proceeding, lives. But God is begetting and begotten, breathing and proceeding. Therefore God lives — John 5:26. FIFTH, from God's outward actions. Whoever vivifies all things lives. But God vivifies all things — Genesis 2:7; Numbers 16:22; 1 Samuel 2:6; Psalm 36:10; Acts 17:25; 1 Timothy 6:13. Therefore God lives.

before: And so that I may seal this first book of our theology with some closing mark, I will here show under the image of a well-born disciple the divine craft and the short way by which the sacred scriptures, as the tables of the Christian kingdom and the roots of true theology, may be read with fruit.

Six things especially are required in a disciple who is to advance far and happily by great daily journeys: (1) age, (2) talent, (3) a faithful teacher, (4) study and labor faithfully to be devoted to the instructor, (5) continual exercise by which he can recite the lesson exactly when the teacher demands it, (6) reverence toward the instructor.
The same things are asked of the student of sacred theology who desires to turn the sacred letters and God's Word to the good of his own soul.
For (1) let him have a firm resolve to put off the old man, that in Christ he may become a new man, indeed a man of God, for whom Sacred Scripture is uniquely destined (Second Timothy 3:16–17).
(2) From God our LORD let him humbly ask with earnest and frequent groans for spiritual understanding and spiritual judgment (James 1:5; Luke 11:9–13).
(3) To JESUS CHRIST, the Master whose chair is in the heavens, let him look with unturned eyes and rightly acknowledge him.
(4) In this divine school let him be assiduous, and not only read but reread what he has read, and with eyes and heart lifted together to heaven meditate and ruminate on what he reads.

(5) Let him weigh one reading against another, render it to the heavenly Master, seek the foundation of truth in him alone, practice by day and by night the doctrine received from him, often remember it, and anxiously ask that he himself may daily become better from himself.

(6) Let him endure under the discipline and correction of Christ and of his Spirit, the heavenly teacher; let him revere and love him, and in his studies seek nothing outside God's glory and his own soul's salvation.
Such a one in Sacred Scripture and theology, or the mysteries of God's kingdom, as θεοδίδακτος — taught by God — will advance most excellently and be blessed forever in heaven.

For this is properly necessary: that whoever desires to understand the sacred letters inwardly and savingly, still more to interpret them for others and apply them with fruit, must first repent, revere God, be willing to acknowledge Christ in his kingdom according to the Spirit and to press his footsteps in the crowd of this world, and ardently ask the spirit of faith and of divine wisdom from him who opened his disciples' mind that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:46).

before: V. The first plague is that which separates the body from her, with which she had been associated from birth by the dearest bond of covenant. This unhappy divorce the impious are accustomed not only to lament tearfully — as Hadrian the Roman emperor: Little soul, wandering, charming, guest and companion of the body, where now do you go? Pale, cold, naked, nor will you give jokes as you used to — but the pious also, although they certainly know they will migrate to the Lord, bear it ill, as Paul testifies (2 Corinthians 5:2): We would not be unclothed, but rather that mortality might be swallowed up by life, without any death namely, as will finally befall those who at the Lord's last coming shall be among the living.

Concerning this, and concerning these inferi, Tertullian in On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 4222: Who, he says, will not desire, while he is in the flesh, to put on immortality over it and to continue life, having gained by death through a vicarious change, lest he experience the underworld that will exact even to the last farthing? For the rest, he will attain the change also after the resurrection, having already experienced the inferi.

before: II. In the essence of GOD the divine names and attributes are to be considered. Many ancients and moderns take the names and attributes of God for the same, so that they also call the essential attributes or properties of God names. But since we ought to study the propriety of words, we preferred here to distinguish the names of God from the essential attributes or properties.

III. Divine names are those by which God is called in the sacred letters, that by them, as far as concerns us, His nature may be explained. The name of God in the Scriptures signifies various things. First, a mark by which God is designated and discerned from creatures (Genesis 32:29; Exodus 3:15 and 14:5). Second, God Himself (Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 5:12 and 7:18 and 20:2 and 116:4; Proverbs 18:10). Third, the power and grace of God (Psalm 118:10-12). Fourth, the will and commandment of God (Deuteronomy 18:19; 1 Samuel 17:45; John 5:43; Luke 24:47). Fifth, the worship, invocation, celebration, profession of God and faith (Micah 4:5; Matthew 28:19; Acts 21:13). We take it here in the first signification.

before: III. Metonymic attributes are those which are said of God by metonymy. Thus God is called firmness — Psalm 18:2; strength — Psalm 22:20; our salvation and help — Psalm 27:1,9 — because He is the author and giver of our firmness, strength, salvation, and help. Thus He is called our song — Exodus 15:2 — because He is the subject of which we sing. And in the same sense our glory — Psalm 3:4; trust — Psalm 65; Jeremiah 17:17; our hope — 1 Timothy 1:1; Jeremiah 14:8.
IV. Ironic attributes are those which are enunciated of God by irony. To this are referred Genesis 3:22; 1 Kings 22:15; Job 38:3 and 40:2; Psalms; Jeremiah 4:10; 1 Corinthians 1:21,25.

before: VIII. But those drawn from other creatures are either common to man and other creatures, or peculiar to these. Common are place, time — Psalm 68; 17. IX. Synecdochic attributes are those attributed to God as it were by synecdoche. Thus the Father is called God, not with exclusion of the Son and Holy Spirit — John; 1 Corinthians 8:6.

And these things concerning Gods attributes, whose perfection is based on the negation of imperfections concerning Him, said both properly and figuratively — concerning which things worthy of observation are those which the Guide of the Perplexed, Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, Moreh Nevukhim, reports: The Law speaks according to the language of the sons of men. Whose sense is: whatever men from the beginning of their thought can attain by their understanding and imagination, that in Scripture is attributed to the Creator. Attributes attributed to God by negation are true attributes; affirmative attributes are greatly imperfect. CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE, On the most holy Trinity, follows.

before: VIII. Through bodily or natural things God also governs human beings — for conserving life, for discipline and punishment, and for benefits and warnings. XI. Further, in a more notable respect God governs humans by teaching when He constitutes covenants among them, and between Himself and them, and acts according to those covenants.

God constituted among humans the covenant of marriage, of which we saw above when teaching the creation of humankind (Genesis 1:28-29; 2:24; Malachi 2:14), which spouses ought to keep between themselves by the faith of chastity and to strengthen by a concordant partnership of useful works. And between Himself and humans God at the beginning constituted the solemn covenant of natural religion (Genesis 1:28-30; 2:16-17; 3:1-4, 22). Here circumspect faith and special obedience toward that law became humans, with the understanding that they were justly punished for their sins, as they also understood themselves obliged to every obedience (Genesis 3:3).

And according to this covenant God so acted that He permitted humans their liberty, as the event makes clear. But they by their own fault, the Devil deceiving, fell into sin, and therefore are justly afflicted by God (Genesis 3; 2 Corinthians 11:3). Hence also they begot offspring after their own likeness (Genesis 5:3; Job 15:14-16; Psalm 51:7; Romans 5:12).

before: Justice of wrath is that by which God most equitably exercises His judgments which He has threatened. Vindicating justice is that by which God destroys the reprobate; this God exercises both in the reprobate of this life and in eternal damnation. Justice of deed is that by which God, whatever He does in decreeing or executing, does conveniently to His infinite rectitude.

Patience is that by which God moderates wrath and punishments. LI. Longsuffering is that by which God suspends wrath, lest He hasten to drive away evil as soon as the creature merits it — Psalm 103:8-9; Nahum 1:3. LII. Meekness is that by which God tempers His wrath, lest it be too great, and lest its severity answer to the magnitude of crimes — Psalm 30:6; 103:10-11; Jeremiah 3:12.

LIV. Clemency is that by which God so moderates due punishments that they by no means surpass the creatures strength, and are much inferior to the merits of sins in gravity and duration — 2 Samuel 7:14-15; Psalm 89:33-34; Joel 2:13; Exodus 22:27. From these things rightly established concerning Gods attributes of the third genus, there follows CHAPTER NINETEEN, On Gods blessedness.

before: XXXVIII. Thus far we have seen how God is accustomed to teach intelligent creatures even compositely: now there follows how He fulfills something concerning the same — namely by effecting, or impeding, or permitting, or tolerating. When God has taught intelligent creatures, if they then do or omit what they ought and as they ought, their obedience is approved by God as good or lawful; if not, it is disapproved as unlawful.

XXXIX. EFFECTING is that by which God brings about those things of which He is the true cause, whether by doing good or by afflicting (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 18:27; 57:3–4; 116:7; Exodus 23:22; Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Haggai 1:6; Psalm 80; 90). XL. IMPEDING is that by which God withdraws from the creature in conservation or concurrence what He wills, and sometimes opposes a stronger force to a weaker, or beyond order strengthens the weaker so that it can stop or drive back the stronger (Genesis 26:6; Isaiah 37:29; Acts 16:6–7).

XLI. PERMISSION is that by which God leaves certain creatures to their own choice. For sometimes He does not impede creatures from acting of themselves, left a little to themselves (Job 1:12; 1 Kings 22:21–22; Acts 14:16). And when God permits them to their own choice, it comes about that if they do not use their wisdom and prudence considerately enough, they fall into sin by their own fault. XLII. TOLERATION is that by which God neither afflicts His creature with punishment nor even with notable benefit. See Matthias Martini's Method published at Herborn and the epitome of methodical theology, book 3, chapters 2–3, printed here.

before: III. Incarnation is that by which the eternal Son of God, human nature having been assumed into the unity of person, at a definite time was made human from a woman, that He might act as mediator between God and humans. Its foundations are shown in Psalm 45:8; Isaiah 7:14; 1 Peter 1:20; John 1:14; Matthew 1:21 and 16:16; Galatians 4:4; 1 John 4:2; 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 2:14. Of this grace the Apostle asserts in 1 Timothy 3:16 that it is the great mystery of godliness.

This incarnation, as we learn from the Scriptures, took place thus: the Holy Spirit coming upon the blessed virgin Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowing her, she conceived and bore the Son of God — that is, an individual and singular human nature, which without male seed, by the omnipotent power common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the virgin had conceived, and which the Son assumed into the unity of person, or, what amounts to the same, personally united to Himself and communicated to that human nature the ultimate substantial term and degree by which an intelligent nature is completed in the category of being

For since a person is a rational nature as incommunicable substance, we call personality that very thing by which a person is constituted in the ultimate and complete personal being, and by which it is made incommunicable. Such personality the nature conceived from the virgin could have had of itself; but lest there be two persons rather than one, the Son of God therefore communicated His own to it and terminated the assumed nature by His first and intimate personal perfection, completed it substantially, and constituted it in the ultimate hypostatic and incommunicable being.

before: XIII. Goodness is that by which God inclines toward communicating good outside Himself. That God is good is testified by Scripture and by all His works — Psalm 34:9; Matthew 19:17; Luke 18:19; Genesis 1:31; against the heresies of Cerdo, Marcion, and the Manicheeseses.

XIV. Benignity is that by which God, by giving some good, shows Himself beneficent to His creatures. The first progression of divine goodness is benignity; one general toward all creatures — Psalm 145:9; Matthew 5:45; another special toward the elect. XV. Grace is that by which God imparts some good to intelligent creatures, regarding none of their merits. Grace excludes the creatures merit; distinctions of grace into operating and cooperating, prevenient, concomitant and subsequent, sufficient and efficacious, we treat elsewhere.

XVI. Gods mercy is the affection of coming to the aid of the miserable, nothing obstructing by reason of sin. Gods mercy is taken actively or passively; here in the former way — Exodus 34:6; Romans 9:18; Ephesians 2:4; Titus 3:5. Just as grace is the second progression of divine goodness excluding merit, so mercy is its third progression, finding a remedy for the miserable.

before: CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX. On those things which were created in the beginning, and namely on the highest heaven, Angels, and earth.

In the beginning God created heaven and earth — Genesis 1:1. Heaven here is taken both properly for the expanse and heavenly things, and figuratively. Figuratively either by metonymy or by synecdoche.

By metonymy: (1) For God its possessor and author — Daniel 4:26; Matthew 21; Luke 15:18,21; John 3:27. (2) For other heaven-dwellers — Job 15:15; Psalm 89:6. (3) For the church militant on earth — Daniel 8:10; Revelation 9:1; 12:7. (4) For meteors — Leviticus 26:19. By synecdoche: (1) For the highest heaven only — Mark 16:19. (2) For the starry heaven — Psalm 19:7. (3) For the air — Genesis 1:26. But in the present heaven is taken by Moses both for the angelic heaven and for the heaven-dwellers produced by God in the beginning: but Earth for the other principle, from which these interior things which the highest heaven encloses — except the rational soul or our immortal spirit — were produced later.

before: XII. Permission is that by which, with divine power temporarily set aside, certain angels are allowed to fall. XIII. Hardening at by which the fallen, grace denied, are made firm in evil.

They are also called unclean spirits (Luke 11:24), worthless spirits (1 Kings 16:14), spirits of error (1 Timothy 4:1), Satan, the Devil, the ancient serpent, the dragon, angels of Satan (Revelation 12:9), father of the lie (John 8:44), spiritual wickedness (Ephesians 6:12), roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), demons (Luke 11), satyrs (Leviticus 17:7), hairy ones (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). The reason for the naming is that they are spirits created by God indeed, but who by free will fell away at the beginning from the truth in which they were made, and became horrible adversaries of both God and human beings, and are kept in eternal chains for judgment (John 8:44; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6).

before: Rufinus in his exposition of the Creed: God is one not by number but by universality — as one sun, so that another cannot be added. Much more is God named one by a word of universality, because there is no other.

This unity of God is manifest in the Scriptures (Deuteronomy 4:35, 39; 6:4; Psalm 18:32; Isaiah 44-48; John 17:3; Romans 3:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4; Galatians 3:20; Ephesians 4:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). Yet to stubborn minds it must be persuaded by reasons known by nature's light. We will not only prove that God is one, but also demonstrate that there cannot be many.

before: II. But in it there is to be considered the object, the condition, and the distinction. III. The object is everything which God, as true and possible being comprehended by His infinite intellect, can freely will. For whatever God can freely will, that same He can also do; and whatever He can do, that same He can freely will.

But God can freely will only those things which are not contrary to His essence and natural will and which can be comprehended by His infinite intellect as true beings, at least as possible. Possibility of a thing is principally from Gods intellect, but formally from the formal reason of things. Hence not because of Gods power, but because of inherent contradiction in the thing, there is no power with respect to contradictories.

And hence God is said to be able to do all possibles which agree with His nature, intellect, and will: all the rest are impossible, because they involve contradiction, impotence, perversity, and falsehood — as to make another God, to be changed, to lie, to sin, to make something simultaneously be and not be. When we deny that these can be done by God, we do not injure His infinite power, but we take care that things incongruous to Gods essence, intellect, and will not be attributed. Compare Luke 1:37; 18:27; Mark 14:36; James 1:17; Psalm 5:5; Numbers 23:19; 2 Timothy 2:13.

before: IV. Original sin is the fault of our nature derived from Adam, consisting of guilt and corruption. Guilt is the obligation to eternal death because of Adams sin imputed to us (Romans 5:12-19). Corruption is the privation of original righteousness and a crooked habit in intellect, will, affections, and the whole human. V. HABITUAL sin is the deformity of the object from the uprightness of the law, remaining in the nature even when the act is not put forth. Hence infants even before actual sin are held by guilt and corruption (Psalm 51:7; Job 14:4; Ephesians 2:3).

before: XI. Seventh, some are concrete, as God, Lord, Father: some abstract, as life, charity, deity. Those teach that God truly subsists: but these that He is a most simple being. XII. And this is the distinction of the divine names.

FIRST is YHWH (Exodus 15:3; Psalm 83:19; Isaiah everywhere). This name is also called the Tetragrammaton and Schemhamphoras. before: IX. Further, the separated soul is not extinguished, but remains. Irenaeus in Against Heresies book 2, chapter 62, draws this chiefly from Christ's narrative: Most fully, he says, the Lord taught that souls persevere in that narration which is written of the rich man and of Lazarus, who was refreshed in Abraham's bosom. The same Christ confirms (Matthew 22:32; Mark 12:26–27; Matthew 10:28; and Luke 12:4 and 23:43); and Stephen (Acts 7:59); and Paul (Romans 8:11 and 14:8; Philippians 1:23).

X. The separated soul does not sleep, but remembers the things it did in this life, and knows what lot awaits it after judgment, and either rejoices in the thought of its felicity or is tormented by the expectation of terrible punishment. Irenaeus gathers this in the same place: Most fully, he says, the Lord taught not only that souls persevere, but also that they remember the works which they did here and from which they ceased, in that narration which is inscribed of the rich man and Lazarus, in which he says the rich man recognizes Lazarus after death, and Abraham likewise. The same the martyrs confirm (Revelation 6:10) and those who follow the Lamb (Revelation 14:4). Whence also Cyprian in his most elegant sermon On Mortality: A great number of dear ones, he says, awaits us there; a frequent and abundant throng of parents, brothers, children desires us — already secure of their own immortality, and still anxious about our salvation.
after: IX. Further, the separated soul is not extinguished, but remains. Irenaeus in Against Heresies book 2, chapter 62, draws this chiefly from Christ's narrative: Most fully, he says, the Lord taught that souls persevere in that narration which is written of the rich man and of Lazarus, who was refreshed in Abraham's bosom. The same Christ confirms (Matthew 22:32; Mark 12:26–27; Matthew 10:28; and Luke 12:4 and 23:43); and Stephen (Acts 7:59); and Paul (Romans 8:10 and 14:8; Philippians 1:23).

X. The separated soul does not sleep, but remembers the things it did in this life, and knows what lot awaits it after judgment, and either rejoices in the thought of its felicity or is tormented by the expectation of terrible punishment. Irenaeus gathers this in the same place: Most fully, he says, the Lord taught not only that souls persevere, but also that they remember the works which they did here and from which they ceased, in that narration which is inscribed of the rich man and Lazarus, in which he says the rich man recognizes Lazarus after death, and Abraham likewise. The same the martyrs confirm (Revelation 6:10) and those who follow the Lamb (Revelation 14:4). Whence also Cyprian in his most elegant sermon On Mortality: A great number of dear ones, he says, awaits us there; a frequent and abundant throng of parents, brothers, children desires us — already secure of their own immortality, and still anxious about our salvation.
